one_liner: Interference-aware core scheduler and kernel-bypass runtime; memcached 99.9% latency 52 us vs 580 ms under Parties* during GC.
what_it_does: Caladan is a CPU scheduler for Linux servers that run latency-critical (LC) services next to best-effort (BE) batch jobs: a root daemon (iokerneld) busy-polls on a dedicated core and moves cores between applications every 10 us, and a kernel module (ksched) carries out the moves. Applications link its Shenango-derived runtime (libruntime.a, libnet.a, libbase.a), which provides green threads, mutex/rwmutex/condvar/waitgroup/RCU, a kernel-bypass TCP/UDP stack with blocking calls (tcp_dial, tcp_listen, tcp_accept, tcp_read, tcp_write, udp_*) and optional SPDK NVMe block I/O (storage_read/storage_write); C++ (rt::Thread, rt::Spawn, rt::TcpConn/TcpQueue/UdpConn) and Rust bindings wrap the C API. Each app states in a config file how many kthreads it may use, how many are guaranteed, and whether it is lc or be. It is neither an event loop nor a sockets drop-in: it replaces the process scheduler and the network stack for the apps it manages.
how_it_is_fast: Parties and Heracles partition hardware (Intel CAT/MBA) and adjust every ~500 ms or more. Caladan reallocates whole cores based on signals it reads every 10 us: the queueing delay of the oldest item in each core's runqueue, NIC RX, storage and timer queues (all in shared memory); global DRAM bandwidth from uncore counters, attributed to tasks by sampling per-core LLC misses; and how long each hyperthread has been on its current request. Three controllers act on these signals. The top-level allocator adds a core to any task over its queueing-delay threshold, the bandwidth controller takes one core per 10 us from the BE task with the most LLC misses while bandwidth is above a limit, and the hyperthread controller idles (mwait) the sibling of an LC request that runs past its threshold, a policy generalized from Elfen scheduling. KSCHED keeps these moves cheap: commands pass through per-core 64-byte shared-memory slots, one multicast IPI kicks many cores, calls are asynchronous, and signal delivery and affinity changes run on the target core. Runtime cores also send and receive their own packets (libibverbs/directpath), so the scheduler core does not forward traffic the way Shenango's did.
when_to_use: A single-socket x86-64 server that colocates microsecond-scale LC services (memcached, RPC, NVMe block storage) with batch jobs whose memory-bandwidth or cache use changes in phases (garbage collection, video encoding, clustering), where 99.9th-percentile latency must stay in the tens of microseconds and batch work should still use the idle cycles.

Several LC and BE tasks on one box with hyperthreads left on. The paper ran 3 LC and 2 BE apps together at up to 230,000 core reallocations/s, with per-task knobs (runtime_qdelay_us, runtime_ht_punish_us, guaranteed vs burstable kthreads).
You control the whole machine and can give iokerneld a physical core, load a kernel module as root, reserve hugepages, and use an NVIDIA/Mellanox ConnectX-4 or newer NIC with directpath.
New C, C++ (gnu++20 bindings) or Rust-nightly services written as blocking green threads, or anything now on Shenango: Caladan is its maintained successor with the same runtime model.
Research on microsecond-scale scheduling: the IOKernel has pluggable policies (ias, simple, experimental numa), and test.sh runs it on a DPDK tap vdev with no real NIC.
when_not_to_use: You need Linux sockets, epoll/io_uring compatibility, TLS or HTTP, or want to keep an existing event-loop server unchanged. Nothing is drop-in: LC services must be ported to its green-thread API, and processes outside the runtime cannot be throttled.

Multi-socket or multi-tenant hosts. It cannot manage interference across NUMA nodes (the numa policy is described as incomplete and experimental), and sharing hyperthread siblings between tasks does nothing against transient-execution attacks; the paper also ran with Meltdown and MDS mitigations off.
WAN or lossy networks. The TCP stack has window scaling and fast retransmit, but I found no congestion-window or SACK code, and the retransmit timeout is fixed at 300 ms with a FIXME comment.

Hardware off the tested path: non-x86 CPUs, ConnectX-3 (dropped; issue #20, 2024), hyperthreading disabled in BIOS (open issue #22), or servers where PCM cannot reach the uncore counters. Non-directpath NICs (ixgbe, i40e and other DPDK PMDs) run, but the maintainers treat that as a testing setup, not a benchmarking one.

LC services that multiplex many connections per thread and cannot be restructured. Without a green thread per connection or per request, extra cores do not help, so the allocator cannot absorb load or interference.

integration.dependencies: git submodules built by `make submodules`: DPDK 25.03 and rdma-core (both patched), Intel PCM (patched), and SPDK (only with CONFIG_SPDK=y). apt packages: libnl-3/libnl-route-3, libnuma, uuid, libssl, libaio, libcunit1, libclang, libncurses, meson, pyelftools and libarchive. Also the ksched kernel module (GPL; fake_idle.ko too when no cpuidle driver is loaded), 2 MB hugepages, the msr module, and the iokerneld daemon run as root. Rust nightly (bindgen 0.69) for loadgen and the Rust bindings. Mellanox OFED 4.6+ and DEVX-capable NIC firmware for directpath.
integration.min_toolchain: GCC by default, or clang with CONFIG_CLANG=y; C is -std=gnu11 and the C++ bindings need -std=gnu++20. The default build adds -muintr, -mxsavec and -mfsgsbase (set CONFIG_NO_UINTR=y for compilers without UINTR), and the default CONFIG_OPTIMIZE=y adds -march=native -flto=auto -ffast-math. No minimum compiler version is documented. Building ksched needs kernel headers. Tested on Ubuntu 18.04 (kernel 5.2) through 24.04 (kernel 6.8).
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux only (kernel 5.0+ for directpath). NICs: its own mlx5 driver for ConnectX-4 and newer is fastest; DPDK PMDs ixgbe, i40e, ice, bnxt, mana (Azure VMs are auto-detected), failsafe, mlx5 and tap are slower; no mlx4/ConnectX-3. It manages one NUMA node, with compile-time limits of 256 CPUs and 4 NUMA nodes. Memory-bandwidth control reads uncore counters through PCM.
integration.thread_safety: Built for multi-core use: green threads migrate between kthreads by work stealing, and the IOKernel can preempt kthreads (signals delivered through ksched, or Intel user interrupts on CPUs with UINTR). Synchronize with the runtime's mutex, rwmutex, condvar, waitgroup, barrier, spinlock and RCU primitives, and wrap per-kthread state in preempt_disable/preempt_enable. Other thread-safety rules are not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — Parties and Linux scheduling manage unmodified processes, but Caladan manages only programs linked against its runtime. pthread batch jobs run unmodified through libshim.a (-Wl,--wrap=main, with no static pthread mutex initializers). LC network services must be ported to its tcp_*/udp_* green-thread API and expose concurrency (a thread per connection or per request), as the authors did for memcached. Programs not using the runtime must run on unmanaged cores.

gotchas: The README says plain `sudo ./iokerneld` runs Shenango's default scheduler and `iokerneld ias` turns on interference control, but current iokernel/main.c picks ias when no policy is given; `simple` is the policy without interference control. The bandwidth controller has a hard-coded 25,000 MB/s default limit (IAS_BW_LIMIT, the paper's value, 70-80% of its test machine's capacity; override it with `bwlimit`). It also needs PCM uncore access, and users who hit 'Can not access server uncore PCI configuration space' (#21) or a resctrl conflict (#35) fell back to `nobw`, which turns off the protection against memory-bandwidth hogs.

Without directpath, the single IOKernel core both forwards packets and runs the controllers. A user on 82599ES NICs could not reproduce the interference isolation until moving to mlx5 with directpath (#35). Each directpath runtime must run as root with a unique IP.

The default CONFIG_OPTIMIZE=y builds with -march=native and -ffast-math, so binaries only run on the build machine's CPU type. Apps must be rebuilt whenever Caladan changes: a mismatched memcached build dropped every packet, and old host_mac/static_arp config lines break TCP on current versions (#30).

Setup is heavy: setup_machine.sh reserves 5,192 2 MB hugepages (~10 GB) on every NUMA node, sets THP to madvise and makes /dev/ksched world-writable, and each green thread reserves a 512 KB stack plus a 512 KB guard. The paper's multicast-IPI speedup came from a patched 5.2 kernel, but today's ksched uses the stock smp_call_function_many, which the paper says costs more under memory-bandwidth interference, so its KSCHED numbers may not carry over to stock kernels.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Shenango for any new work: same runtime model, still maintained, directpath removes the IOKernel packet bottleneck, and it adds memory-bandwidth and hyperthread interference control. Pick it over IX, mTCP, F-Stack or Demikernel when the goal is colocating microsecond-scale services with batch jobs on shared cores rather than peak throughput for one app on dedicated cores; if you only need a faster event loop on stock Linux sockets, the io_uring siblings (monoio, Condy) need no dedicated core, kernel module or porting.
verified_claims_summary: OSDI '20 paper, run on one socket of a dual 12-core Xeon Broadwell server (exact model not given) with a 40 GbE ConnectX-5 and a kernel 5.2 patched for faster multicast IPIs, with security mitigations off and no compiler stated. With memcached 1.5.6 (USR mix, 800k req/s) next to a Boehm-GC PARSEC swaptions job, Caladan kept 99.9th-percentile latency (20 ms windows) near 52 us through GC cycles, while the authors' own Parties reimplementation (Parties*, given the same kernel-bypass runtime and hyperthreads) peaked at 580 ms (11,000x) and got 5% less batch throughput. Linux (kernel TCP on 5.4, BE at SCHED_IDLE) and Shenango appear only in a graph, where stream-DRAM interference raised each one's tail latency 235x and 6x over its own no-interference run. A microbenchmark comparing ksched with Linux syscalls showed 43x less scheduler work, 5x lower latency when moving 22 tasks, and 560k vs ~285k core reallocations/s.
status_note: Actively maintained by the MIT authors (last main-branch commit 2026-05-10, maintainers reply to most issues, tested through Ubuntu 24.04/kernel 6.8) and Apache-2.0 with a GPL kernel module; it is a platform you deploy on a dedicated machine rather than a library to vendor, and the paper's artifact repo (caladan-all) has fallen behind the main repo.
